zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); [dataset documentation](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription and physical lineation are based on the supplied BnF scan, not copied from the lexical index.

lines.note: Kidoguchi is the entrance or gate of a barrier, as the Portuguese explicitly explains. The initial is an ordinary roman Q belonging to the headword, not italic O followed by a separate word.

runs.text: O trazer ſempre o meſmo vestido.

lines.note: Kidōshi denotes continually wearing the same clothing. The scan has meſmo, without the extra i introduced by recognition; the historical Japanese spelling is retained.
The example describes wearing one's clothes continuously. The caron belongs to Ixǒ, and Portuguese ſẽ- continues into pre on the next row; the abbreviation mark is not expanded in the transcription.
This completes the explanation as always wearing one and the same garment. The closing B. is an upright usage label rather than part of the italic translation.
Kiha is explained by sute, yaburu: discarding and tearing up. The Portuguese likewise begins with breaking or tearing and throwing away, completed by fora below.

runs.text: fora como papeis, ou conhecimento que ja não

lines.note: The objects are papers or a written acknowledgement that is no longer useful. Conhecimento is being used for a document here, not abstract knowledge; the sentence continues on the following row.
The example names a written acknowledgement and a litigation petition. The comma after Xacujǒ separates the listed documents, while meyaſu has the long-s form visible in the scan.
Nado wo kiha suru completes the Japanese example of tearing up and discarding such documents. The Portuguese reads botar, not OCR botor, and its por hi construction continues below.
The objects discarded are acknowledgements and litigation papers. Hi completes por hi from the previous row; it is Portuguese running text, not a Japanese fragment.
Kihan is paraphrased as modoru fune, a returning vessel. The scan supports Modoru fune rather than the malformed OCR and kana hint Modoiù fure.

Torna completes the definition of a vessel returning. The upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the Portuguese sentence. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Palaura que ſe eſcreue nos ſobre eſcri-

lines.note: This first Qifen entry concerns a term written in letter superscriptions. The physical division eſcri- / tos is retained rather than joining the word across rows.

runs.text: tos das cartas: como quem diz, reposta pera

lines.note: The superscription is explained approximately as a reply addressed to the recipient. Reposta is retained as the printed historical form; no expected s is inserted before p.

runs.text: voßa merce, &c. posto que nas cartas dos

lines.note: The phrase is equivalent to addressing your worship or your honour. Posto que introduces the restriction completed on the next line; voßa retains the supplied diplomatic ligature representation.

runs.text: ſeculares, fora da Igreja não corre eſta palaura.

lines.note: The compiler says this expression does not circulate in secular letters outside the Church. This is the dictionary's own usage claim, not an added claim about all contemporary correspondence.
The second Qifen entry gives the honorific address directly. Enlargement supports mercè with a final grave-accented e, not the OCR's mertẽ.
Kihō is paraphrased as an honoured person or party, and Idem refers to the preceding honorific address. Its caron is kept distinct from the circumflex of the following entry.

This separate homophonous entry is a country in danger, explicitly ayauki kuni. The Portuguese ar- begins arriſcado on the next physical row; the circumflex is not harmonized with the preceding headword.

runs.text: riſcado a ſe perder, ou deſtruir.

lines.note: The kingdom is at risk of being lost or destroyed. The printed consonant cluster supports deſtruir rather than OCR deſruir; the first syllable of arriſcado remains on the preceding row.

runs.text: Palaura que ſe eſcreue nos ſobre eſcri-

lines.note: Another Qifô is a respectful letter-superscription expression. The scan supplies a circumflex over o that the OCR omitted; this is kept separate from the neighbouring senses.

runs.text: tos das cartas falando com reſpeito.

lines.note: This completes the definition as a respectful form used on letters. Reſpeito restores the visible p misread as t, without changing the historical long-s spelling.

runs.text: Ponta da frecha feita de cana.

lines.note: This entry denotes an arrow point made of cane. Feita means made, not OCR ſeita. The worn mark over o is read as a circumflex after comparison with the nearby types; the supplied NINJAL headword index also identifies Qifô, but does not replace the scan as authority.

runs.text: O dar à Tera, ou mosteiro renda de ter-

lines.note: Kifu is donating income from land to a temple or monastery. The headword begins Q, not G; Tera is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation. The divided ter- continues as terras.

runs.text: ras, ou varzeas, ou outra couſa. ¶

lines.note: The donation may consist of land, cultivated lowlands, or another thing. After the paragraph mark, Qifu begins the Japanese example completed by ſuru on the next row.

runs.text: Dar Chiguiô à Tera, ou outra couſa.

lines.note: Qifu suru is illustrated by giving a landholding or other property to a temple. Chiguiô and Tera occur inside the Portuguese sentence; the visible mark on Chiguiô is a circumflex, not OCR grave ò.

This Qifu concerns skin or the bodily surface, distinct from the donation entry. The repeated fadaye is retained as printed; the scan's damaged letters do not warrant replacing the Japanese paraphrase.
The short continuation specifies the human body as the surface under discussion. It belongs to the skin entry and is not a separate headword or page furniture.

Kifuku is cross-referred to Qibucu, then illustrated by soldiers submitting. The cross-reference includes an i omitted by OCR; Xiſot retains its final checked consonant rather than being expanded to a modern syllabic spelling.

Kotogotoku completes the divided adverb, and the soldiers respectfully submit. The verb reads xitatematçureba, with e rather than OCR o in the conditional ending. Taif. is the upright source label retained in its visible abbreviated form.
Book 28 is cited before the translation: all the soldiers yielding and submitting. The full stop after 28 and the word boundary in Os ſoldados are visible and restored.
The reflexive verb completes the description of the soldiers submitting themselves. This short continuation belongs to the cited example rather than a separate entry.

Kigan is paraphrased as returning wild geese; the Portuguese calls the bird a wild duck returning to colder regions. The two language descriptions are preserved without imposing a modern zoological identification.
Na completes torna, describing the bird's return toward cold regions. The physical tor- / na division is preserved, and the line closes the preceding Qigan entry.
Kigane is directly glossed as gold. This is an independent one-line entry, and the simple Portuguese noun does not require a supplied example or additional wording.
Kigasa denotes greatness of heart. The scan supports Qigaſa rather than OCR Cagaſa; the repeated form begins an example across the printed hyphen.
The example describes a person possessing greatness of heart. The Portuguese offers a person of great heart and continues with the alternative grandioſo below.
Grandioſo completes the preceding characterization as magnanimous or grand in spirit. The brief line remains attached to the example rather than being absorbed into the next headword.
Kigaruna is followed by the preferred expression ki no karui hito. Fito, not OCR fio, supplies person; the Portuguese characterization continues below. Meliùs is italic editorial apparatus.
The person is cheerful, ready, or alert. Enlargement gives alegre and prompta rather than OCR ategre and prompia, agreeing with the preceding Japanese explanation.
Kigawa is hide or leather dyed yellow. The initial Q and following letters form a single headword; the OCR's intervening space is not a separate Japanese word.
Kigae denotes clothing for changing into. Qi- starts the repeated noun in the example on the following physical row; the scan preserves an actual terminal hyphen.
Kigae wo motasuru means having someone carry a change of clothes. The causative interpretation is supplied by fazer leuar; the Portuguese phrase continues below.
These are spare clothes for changing. The historical printed ſobreſelente is retained rather than modernizing the word or inserting expected consonants.
Kigen concerns countenance or mood. The example begins hito no kigen; the scan supports Fitono, not OCR Firoro, and Sembrante rather than Senbrante.
The completed example is pleasing someone or trying to humour them. The Portuguese compra- continues as comprazer across the row break; it is not the separate noun for a purchase.
The first translation ends with pleasing someone; the next example concerns showing a good mood. Mo- begins Mostrar, whose remainder is on the final row of the column.
The translation says to show a good, cheerful countenance. After the paragraph mark, Qiguenuo begins a new example whose verb continues at the top of column 2; it is body text, not a catchword.

Sokonō completes Qiguenuo from the preceding column: displeasing someone or spoiling their mood. The first vowel is o, and the Portuguese reads Deſcontentar with a long s; the nasal abbreviation in alguẽ is retained.
The continuation explains causing someone to have an unhappy countenance. This closes the cross-column example under Qiguen rather than introducing a new entry.
This Qigui means different opinions or individual inclinations, paraphrased as kokorogokoro. Its initial is Q, not the OCR's D.
The alternative Portuguese gloss is wills or wishes. This short line completes the preceding entry and remains a separate physical row.
The next Qigui means trees; the example is their twig tips or treetops. The scan reads Qiguino cozuye, restoring both the missing i and the z misrecognized by OCR.
The translation identifies the tips of the trees' small branches. This supports cozuye in the Japanese example without replacing the dictionary's spelling with modern romanization.

runs.text: Boninas, ou flores de cor amarela.

lines.note: Kigiku is described as yellow flowers. The Portuguese botanical wording is retained without extending the entry into a modern species identification.

Kigyō is glossed as sentient living beings. S. is the separate upright written-register label; the caron over the headword's final o remains visible. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kigisu is equated with kiji and glossed as a woodland fowl. The headword begins Qigui-, not OCR Qugui-; B. is retained as an upright usage label.

runs.text: Condição boa, ou ruim, ou poſtura.

lines.note: Kigiwa concerns good or bad disposition, or bearing and posture. Both senses are introduced here and separately illustrated in the following rows.
The first example describes a person of good disposition. Its Portuguese adjective phrase continues into condição on the next row.
The first person is good-natured and generous. The second example begins with hakama and changes the focus to how the clothing sits or is worn; qigui- continues below.
The divided Japanese phrase describes someone with a good hakama appearance. The Portuguese says graceful and well turned out, completed by the reference to breeches below.
This completes the clothing example with breeches. The scan supports e, not OCR a, and places the nasal mark over that e in calçoẽs; it is not normalized to modern calções.
Kigo denotes carefully adorned and arranged words. The purpose of that polished wording is supplied on the next row; the actual concerta- division is retained.

The words are arranged to flatter. Liſongear preserves the historical spelling, and the final upright S. marks written usage rather than belonging to the italic gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Ripas de pao que poem ſobre os

lines.note: Kigomai denotes wooden laths laid over roof timbers. The Portuguese relative clause continues with the supporting timbers on the next line.
Aguieiros supplies the roof members over which the laths are placed. The uncommon historical Portuguese form is retained as printed, rather than replaced with a modern construction term.

runs.text: Armas como ſaya de malha que ſe

lines.note: Kigomi is protective armour such as a mail garment. Here armas refers to defensive equipment, and the following row explains that it is worn beneath other clothes.

runs.text: veste de baixo dos outros veſtidos.

lines.note: The armour is worn underneath the other garments. The printed de baixo remains two words, and the locally supplied st/ſt distinction is not globally regularized.
Kigotnai characterizes someone harsh or rough in speech. The unusual tn sequence is visible and retained rather than silently changing the historical Japanese form.
The example describes that person's rough manner of speaking. The repeated adjective reads qigotnai, confirming the headword and correcting OCR qigomnai.
Mono iygia completes the example about a person's speech. Aquelle is one Portuguese word in the scan, not the OCR's A quelle; the description of the manner of speech follows below.
This completes the translation as a harsh, rustic way of speaking. It explains the adjective through behaviour rather than identifying the speaker's place of origin.
The adverb corresponding to Qigotnai is now illustrated. Both occurrences read Qigotnǒ, retaining the visible tn cluster and caron; the OCR's second Qigomǒ is corrected.

runs.text: uo yǔ. i, Cotobani cadouo araxete yǔ.

lines.note: The example is speaking harshly, paraphrased as giving one's words an edge. The two yǔ forms preserve their carons; the Japanese paraphrase remains roman rather than becoming Portuguese apparatus.
The Portuguese translates the manner of speaking as sharp, harsh, or rustic. Ruſticamente is a single printed word; the OCR's internal space is removed.
The gloss adds lack of refinement or gentleness. These qualities complete the rough-speech definition and do not open a new entry.

runs.text: Meſas brancas com ſeus pees feitas de

lines.note: Kigu denotes plain light-coloured tables furnished with legs. The material and unfinished condition are specified on the next physical row.

The tables are made of hinoki and described as not yet worked or planed. Finoqi is Japanese embedded in an otherwise Portuguese explanation; its visible italic setting is retained for optional human typeface review.
Kigurushii describes something distressing or sad, or the state of feeling that way. The Portuguese alternative continues into the following line.
The continuation describes sadness and an unpleasant disposition or condition. The scan supplies the i omitted in OCR trſte.
Kigurushisa is the corresponding noun for distress or discomfort. It is printed alone as a derivative of the preceding adjective, with no Portuguese words to supply.
Kigurushū is the corresponding adverbial form. The scan reads Qi-, not OCR Qu-, and the final u carries a caron; the separately indented derivative remains on its own row.
Kiga is explained through rising and lying down. Voqi represents the rising action, while fuſu means lying down; the Portuguese likewise pairs getting up with remaining recumbent.
Deitado completes the lying-down part of the definition. The final S. is the upright written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kijin is returning from a military campaign or camp, paraphrased by jin yori kaeru. The headword's printed g is retained; guer- begins Portuguese guerra across the physical break.
Ra completes guerra, after which the example gives the verbal expression Qigin ſuru. The space between those two printed words is retained, and Vt. is italic apparatus.

This ki-i is an honoured person's will or command, paraphrased by tattoqi cocoro and Guio-i. Both internal hyphens are visible linguistic word notation, not line-break markers; OCR Qiai and Guio.i are corrected.

runs.text: do do ſenhor, ou de peßoa honrada.

lines.note: The command comes from a lord or an honoured person. Manda- / do is one Portuguese word divided between rows, followed by the separate preposition do.
The next ki-i is a marvellous or strange thing, explicitly fushigina koto. Its internal hyphen is retained separately from the terminal division of Portuguese marauilhoſa.
The adjectival example Qijna coto repeats the sense of something marvellous and astonishing. Idem refers back to that definition, not to the previous honourific-command entry.
The example describes experiencing astonishment. The paragraph mark omitted by OCR is visible at the left; the Japanese phrase and Portuguese infinitive continue the same entry.
Muito completes the translation as being greatly astonished. The short row is body text and not a catchword.
Kiin means returning to a temple. The scan reads Teraye, not OCR Toraye; Tera in the Portuguese sentence is the Japanese temple term. The printed headword spacing is retained.

runs.text: O eſtar algũa couſa ao parecer, ou

lines.note: Kizen here concerns something being subject to someone's judgement or wishes. The gloss continues below; algũa retains its printed nasal abbreviation.

This completes the gloss with someone's will and gives Qijenni ari as the example. The scan corrects OCR Contade and Cijenni, and the final character is the upright usage label S., not ô. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
